words.g: is wound up and put away

1.sense: The surah opens on a condition and does not finish the sentence for thirteen verses. Kuwwirat is the verb for winding a turban round the head, gathering cloth in on itself. The sun, the one arrival that has never failed in any human lifetime, is bundled up and taken out of service.

notes.t: The root k-w-r is the wrapping of cloth. The lexicographers also give a sense of being gathered up and thrown down. Under either reading the light is collected inward rather than switched off, which is a different picture from a lamp going out.

A report attributed to Ibn Umar has the Prophet ﷺ saying that whoever wants to look at the Day of Resurrection as though he were seeing it should recite this surah along with Al-Infitar and Al-Inshiqaq. The chains are discussed and the gradings given to it differ.
notes.src: Tirmidhi in the chapters of tafsir, and Ahmad; graded hasan by some and weakened by others

notes.t: The twelve conditions of verses one to thirteen are usually divided in two: the first six happen to this world as it ends, and the last six happen after it. Nothing in the text marks the seam, but the subject matter changes at the pairing of souls.

links.why: the moon eclipsed and the sun and moon brought together
the same list of conditions answered by one sentence about the self

2.sense: The stars go next. The verb carries falling and also going turbid, the way clear water clouds. Between this verse and the one before it, both of the fixed references a person used to find his position and his hour have been removed.

notes.t: Inkadara is used of a bird stooping down out of the sky onto its prey, and of water losing its clearness. The exegetes keep both senses here: the stars come down, and their light thickens.
The Qur'an elsewhere states that the stars were set in place so that people could find their way by them on land and at sea.

links.why: the same event in one word, and when the stars scatter
what the stars were for, which is what is being cancelled

3.sense: Mountains are the standard the language uses for what does not move. Here they are made to travel, and the verb is the ordinary one for setting a caravan on the road. They are not smashed in this verse. They are walked off.

notes.t: The Qur'an gives several statements about the mountains on that Day: set moving here, made into a scattered dust elsewhere, and reduced to a mirage in another place. Whether these are stages of one process or separate descriptions of one event is not settled by the text.
notes.src: at-Tabari records the positions of the early exegetes and does not choose between them

notes.t: The mountains are named in the Qur'an as pegs driven into the earth to steady it. Setting them moving undoes the specific job the Book assigns them.

links.why: the mountains scattered and the earth left a bare level plain
the sky opened as gateways and the mountains turned to mirage

words.g: the she-camels ten months with young

4.sense: One line of ordinary Arabian accounting drops into the middle of the cosmos coming apart. A she-camel in her tenth month was the single most valuable thing a man in that audience could own. On that day she stands loose in the open and her owner walks past her.

notes.t: Ishar is the plural of ushara, a camel ten months gone with young and days away from a birth that would make her worth more than everything else in the tent. The verse does not say the Day is terrible. It says nobody came for her.

The verb is not destroyed but neglected, put out of use. The property survives and the attachment to it does not, which is the same move the Qur'an makes when it says a nursing mother will forget the child at her breast.

This is the only one of the twelve conditions drawn from the audience's own economy rather than from the sky. It is placed fourth, between the mountains and the wild animals, so that the reader meets it without warning.

links.why: every nursing mother forgetting what she nursed, the same abandonment of what was most held
the man who flees his brother, his mother and his father on that Day

5.sense: Animals that spend their whole lives keeping distance from each other and from people are brought into one place. The verb is hashr, the word used everywhere else in the Qur'an for the mustering of humanity, and it is spent here on beasts.

notes.t: The Prophet ﷺ said that rights will be restored to those they belong to on the Day of Resurrection, to the point that the hornless sheep will have its claim settled against the horned one. Whatever else the gathering of the animals is for, a settling of accounts among them is established.
notes.src: Muslim, from Abu Hurayra, in the Book of Virtue and Good Manners

notes.t: The Qur'an states that no creature on the earth and no bird flying on its wings is anything other than a community like your own, and that they are gathered to their Lord.

What becomes of the animals after that gathering was disputed by the early exegetes, some holding that they are turned to dust once the claims between them are settled. The Qur'an does not say, and the reports about it are not of one weight.
notes.src: at-Tabari collects the reports from the early exegetes without settling on one

links.why: animals as communities with a Lord and a gathering of their own
everything in creation already has a relation to Him that people do not hear

6.sense: The seas are made to burn, or to swell and run into each other until they are one body of water. Either way the element that puts fire out is the one being described, and it is not behaving as water.

notes.t: Sujjirat has been read as kindled into fire, as filled until overflowing, and as emptied out. The first is the most common because the verb is used of stoking an oven, and the same root gives the sea described elsewhere as al-bahr al-masjur.
notes.src: at-Tabari records the several readings from the early exegetes; the root is the one used for firing an oven

notes.t: The Qur'an says elsewhere that the seas are burst forth on that Day, using a different verb for what may be the same event.

links.why: the seas erupting, listed among the same conditions
an oath sworn by the sea filled with fire, the same root

7.sense: Souls are sorted and matched. From this verse onward the twelve conditions stop describing the world and start describing what happens to people, and the first thing that happens to them is that they are put with their own kind.

notes.t: Three readings run through the commentaries: each soul is joined to the sort of person it resembles, or each soul is returned to the body it left, or each soul is paired with the deeds it sent ahead. The verb supports all three and the text does not narrow it.
notes.src: reports from Ibn Abbas and others, collected by at-Tabari, point in more than one direction

notes.t: The Qur'an sorts people into three ranks elsewhere and uses the same word, azwaj, for the sorting. That parallel is the strongest argument for reading this verse as classification rather than reunion with the body.

links.why: humanity divided into three kinds, using the same word for kind
gather those who did wrong and the ones of their sort

8.sense: In the middle of a list about suns and seas, one child. Arabs of that time buried unwanted infant daughters in the sand. The verse does not turn to the fathers. It turns to her, and she is the one given a voice in the proceedings.

notes.t: The grammar carries the argument. The person who was silenced is the one called on to speak, and the man who silenced her is not addressed at all. He has to stand there while the question is put to her in his hearing.
The Prophet ﷺ named the burying of daughters among the things Allah has forbidden, in the same breath as disobedience to mothers and the withholding of what is owed.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from al-Mughira ibn Shuba

notes.t: The Qur'an describes the practice from the father's side elsewhere: his face darkens at the news of a daughter, he hides from his people, and he decides between keeping her in humiliation and putting her in the dust.

links.why: the same act described from inside the father's calculation
do not kill your children fearing poverty, with the reason given

9.sense: The question itself, and it cannot be answered. There is no crime available to name, because she had not lived long enough to commit one. The Arabic asks for a specific offence, bi-ayyi dhanb, and the absence of any is the whole of the verdict.

notes.t: An unanswerable question in Arabic argument functions as a sentence. Nothing further is said about the killer in this surah, and nothing needs to be, because the question has already been asked in front of everyone.

The exegetes divide over whether the question is really addressed to the girl or, through her, to the one who buried her. Both readings are early, and neither changes the outcome for the man standing beside her.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both positions among the early exegetes

notes.t: Dhanb is a specific fault, not guilt in general. The word choice narrows the demand: name the thing she did.

links.why: the prohibition set out among the things your Lord has forbidden
the soul Allah made sacred, not to be killed except by right

10.sense: The records are opened. Nushirat is what you do to a rolled scroll or a folded cloth, which is to unroll it where it can be seen. The point is not that a record exists but that it is being opened in public.

notes.t: Publication is the load-bearing idea. A private ledger held against a person is one thing; a page spread open in an assembly is another, and the Qur'an consistently describes the second.
The Qur'an has the record handed to its owner with the instruction to read it himself and the statement that he is a sufficient accountant against himself today.

links.why: read your own record, you are enough of an auditor today
the book that left out nothing small or large

11.sense: Kashata is the verb for skinning an animal, pulling the hide back off the carcass. The sky is not opened here and not torn. It is removed as a covering is removed, which implies it was covering something.

notes.t: The word belongs to butchery and to the peeling of a skin or a cover off what is underneath. Its use makes the sky a surface rather than a place, and makes what is behind it the subject of the sentence.
The Qur'an says the sky will be rolled up as a scribe rolls up written sheets, which is a related picture of a surface being handled rather than destroyed.

links.why: the heaven rolled up the way a scribe rolls a written sheet
We have removed your covering, so your sight today is sharp

12.sense: The fire is not lit at this moment. It is stoked, which assumes it was already burning. The doubled form of the Arabic verb is the form used for intensifying something, so the verse describes an increase rather than an ignition.

notes.t: Arabic verbs of this pattern add force to a base meaning, and the same shape has already been used three times in this surah for the sun, the mountains and the seas. The heat is being turned up on something that has been there.
Elsewhere the Qur'an says the Fire is brought into plain view for those who deviated and for whoever has eyes to see, which is a different verb but the same moment.

links.why: the Fire brought into view for those who went astray, one verse before the Garden
the Fire displayed for whoever sees

13.sense: The twelfth and last condition, and the only one in the list that is good news. The Garden is moved toward the people rather than the people being marched toward it, which reverses the direction of every other approach in the surah.

notes.t: Zulfa is nearness, and the verb is passive: something moves it. In a list where everything else has been unwound, stripped, scattered or stoked, this is the one item that arrives.
The Qur'an pairs the Fire being displayed and the Garden being brought near in more than one surah, always in that order, so that the good news lands last.

links.why: the Garden brought near to the God-fearing, not far off
the same pairing of Garden and Fire in the reverse order of display

14.sense: Twelve conditions, and the answer is four words. All of that machinery so that one person can find out what they brought. The word for soul is left indefinite, which in Arabic makes it each soul, singly, rather than everyone at once.

notes.t: The payoff is deliberately small after the size of what came before. The universe is taken apart and the result is a piece of private knowledge arriving inside one person.
Ahdarat is to bring a thing and make it present, not simply to do it. The deeds are not remembered on that Day. They are produced and set down.
The Qur'an uses the same root when it says that every soul will find what it did of good made present before it, and what it did of evil too.

links.why: the same root for deeds made present, with the wish for distance from them
a soul will know what it sent ahead and what it held back

15.sense: The second half of the surah begins with an oath, and the oath is sworn by things that withdraw. Khunnas is from a verb meaning to draw back and disappear from where you were standing.

notes.t: The particle la before uqsimu looks like a negation and is not one. Most grammarians read it as an intensifier that strengthens the oath, and the same construction opens two other surahs. A minority read it as denying something the audience had just claimed.
notes.src: the grammarians differ; the same opening occurs at 75:1 and 90:1

notes.t: What al-khunnas are is not fixed by the text. The reading most often given from the early exegetes is the planets, which appear to slow and reverse against the fixed stars and then vanish by day. Others read it as the stars in general.
notes.src: reports from Ali and Ibn Abbas favour the planets; at-Tabari lists the other views

links.why: an oath by the setting places of the stars, called a great oath if you knew
another oath sworn on the twilight, the night and the moon as it fills

words.g: the ones that go to cover

16.sense: Two more words for the same objects. They run their course and then back into hiding. Between this verse and the one before it the sworn-by things appear, travel and disappear, and they do it on a schedule nobody set for them.

notes.t: Kunnas comes from kinas, the covert or lair a gazelle backs into. The image is not of something switching off but of an animal going into its den and coming out again at the same hour.

The three descriptions across verses fifteen and sixteen are read together as one set of objects rather than three. Whether that set is the five visible planets, the stars generally, or, on a minority reading, wild cattle and deer, the exegetes did not agree.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir record all three identifications from the early generations

links.why: Ibrahim watching star, moon and sun set and refusing to serve what disappears
the sun running to a fixed term and the moon measured out in stages

words.g: it draws on, or draws away

17.sense: The verb means both the coming of the night and its going. Arabic has a class of words that hold opposite meanings, and this is one of them. The oath does not choose, and the choice is left sitting next to the dawn in the following line.

notes.t: Because the next verse is about morning, many exegetes take asasa as the night turning away rather than arriving. Others keep both senses on the grounds that the word is one of the addad, the words that carry a meaning and its reverse.
notes.src: at-Tabari reports both from the early exegetes; the lexicographers class the word among the addad

notes.t: The doubled sound of the root, ain sin ain sin, imitates something that moves in stages rather than at once. Night does not fall in Arabic here. It creeps.

links.why: an oath by the night when it covers and the day when it shows itself
by the night when it retreats and the morning when it brightens

18.sense: The dawn breathes. Nafas is the breath in the chest, and the verb turns first light into an inhalation taken after the held breath of the night. The verse describes something anyone awake before fajr has felt: the air changes before the light does.

notes.t: Tanaffasa is the reflexive of the verb for breathing, so the morning is doing it to itself rather than being blown on. It is the one word in this oath section that is not about vanishing.
The Qur'an calls Allah the one who splits the daybreak open, faliq al-isbah, which is a harder image than this one for the same moment.

links.why: the splitter of the dawn, the same event under a different verb
an oath on the daybreak and on the night as it passes

19.sense: This is what the oaths were for. What you are hearing is carried by a noble messenger. The Arabic says the speech of a messenger, not the speech from one, and a rasul by definition delivers what he was given rather than what he thought of.

notes.t: Who the noble messenger is here was disputed. The three descriptions that follow, strength, a settled place with the Owner of the Throne, and being obeyed there, lead most exegetes to Jibril, and verse twenty two then turns to the Prophet ﷺ separately as your companion.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir both prefer Jibril; a minority of exegetes read it of the Prophet ﷺ

notes.t: The construction rules out authorship in one phrase. Whatever else is argued about the Qur'an, this verse does not claim that the one saying it composed it.
Surat al-Haqqa uses almost the same sentence and then spends four verses ruling out the alternatives, ending with a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.

links.why: the same phrase followed by the same set of denials
it is only a revelation revealed, taught by one of great strength

20.sense: Three things are said about the carrier, and all three are about the safety of what he carries. He is strong enough to hold it, he stands with the Owner of the Throne, and his standing there is not provisional.

notes.t: Makin comes from makana, to have a fixed position. The word describes a fixture rather than a favourite, someone whose place does not depend on how the last errand went.
The same angel is described in Surat an-Najm as one of great powers and sound strength, and in Surat ash-Shuara as the trustworthy Spirit who brought it down onto the Prophet ﷺ's ﷺ heart.

links.why: taught to him by one intense in strength, of sound faculty
the trustworthy Spirit named as the one who brought it down

21.sense: Obeyed there, and trustworthy. The two words face in opposite directions: he has authority over others in the place he stands, and he holds back nothing from the One who sent him. A message can fail at either end and neither end fails here.

notes.t: Amin is the same word the Makkans had been using of the Prophet ﷺ himself for years before any revelation came. The chain from the Throne to the audience is described in terms of trust at every link in it.

Thamma means there, pointing back to the place named in the previous verse. The obedience described is in the heavenly assembly, not on earth, which is part of why most exegetes read these verses of an angel.
notes.src: the exegetes read thamma as pointing to the place named in verse twenty; the identification of the messenger follows from it

links.why: the phrase a trustworthy messenger, used by prophet after prophet to their people
Musa to Pharaoh, using the same two words about himself

22.sense: The charge of madness is answered by naming a relationship instead of arguing. He is not a stranger arriving with a claim. He is your sahib, the man whose company you have kept, whose forty years in your streets you watched.

notes.t: The Qur'an declines to use his name here. Sahib puts the burden on the audience's own memory of him, which is evidence they already hold and cannot pretend not to.

Majnun is not a general insult. It means struck by the jinn, and it was the Makkan explanation for a man producing speech he could not have produced, which is why the surah answers it beside the charge about a devil's speech three verses later.
The Qur'an makes the same denial in other surahs, once addressed directly to the Prophet ﷺ and once put to the audience as a challenge to reflect on him.

links.why: you are not, by the favour of your Lord, possessed
stand and reflect, there is no madness in your companion

23.sense: He saw him. Not was told, not felt, saw, and the verse says where and adds that the horizon was clear, which rules out a shape half made out in bad light.

notes.t: Most exegetes read the seen one as Jibril in his created form, since the surah has just spent four verses describing him. Surat an-Najm describes what appears to be the same sighting on the highest horizon.

Whether the Prophet ﷺ ever saw his Lord with his eyes was disputed among the Companions themselves. Aisha denied it firmly, and Ibn Abbas is transmitted as holding that he saw Him with his heart. This verse was not the main ground of that dispute, but it gets pulled into it.
notes.src: Aisha's denial is in Bukhari and Muslim; the report from Ibn Abbas is in Muslim

notes.t: Mubin here describes the horizon, not the seeing. The Arabic makes the conditions of the sighting part of the claim.

links.why: the same sighting told at length, with the heart not denying what it saw
a second sighting, at the lote tree of the boundary

24.sense: He does not ration it. A man holding news that nobody else can obtain has every reason to release it selectively, and this verse says he passed on all of it, including the parts that cost him standing.

notes.t: Two canonical readings stand here and both are recited. Hafs from Asim, the reading of this Mushaf, has danin with dad, meaning stingy with it. Other readers among the ten have zanin with za, meaning suspected concerning it. Both were transmitted, and the two senses are close enough that neither reading disturbs the other.
notes.src: the canonical readings; Hafs reads danin with dad, and other canonical readers read zanin with za

notes.t: The strongest evidence for the claim is inside the Qur'an itself. It preserves verses that correct the Prophet ﷺ in public, including a reproach for turning away from a blind man in favour of a chief. A filtered message would not have kept those.

links.why: a correction of the Prophet ﷺ that was transmitted rather than withheld
what would have happened had he attributed anything to Us that We did not say

25.sense: The third charge closed. Not madness, not withholding, and not a devil's whisper. The Makkans had a working category for a man receiving words from an unseen source, the kahin who took his lines from a jinn, and this verse refuses the category rather than arguing inside it.

notes.t: The Qur'an answers this charge at length in another surah: the devils did not bring it down, it is not fit for them, they are not capable of it, and they are barred from listening.
Rajim means pelted and driven away, and it ties back to the stars sworn by earlier in this same surah, since the Qur'an describes eavesdroppers on the heavenly assembly being driven off by them.

links.why: the same denial argued out in four verses
the jinn finding the sky guarded and any listener met with a piercing flame

26.sense: Three explanations have been named and shut, and the verse asks where there is left to walk. It is not a rhetorical flourish about being misguided. It is the plain question you put to someone who stands up and leaves in the middle of a conversation.

notes.t: The Arabic does not say where are you going wrong. It says where are you going, and leaves the destination blank because there is not one to name.
The Qur'an supplies the answer in another surah, where a man asks on that Day where the escape is and is told there is no refuge and the settling place is with his Lord.

links.why: the same question asked by the fleeing man, and answered
respond before a Day comes with no turning back and no denying it

27.sense: After three denials, the statement of what it is. A reminder, which assumes the hearer knew it once and let it go, and a reminder addressed to everyone rather than to one tribe holding one sanctuary.

notes.t: Dhikr claims recovery rather than novelty. A reminder is not new information, and calling the Book one places the argument on ground the listener already stands on.
For all the worlds is a wide address to have been recited in Makka, where the audience was a handful of clans and the Prophet ﷺ had no state and few followers.
The same sentence closes two other surahs word for word, in both cases immediately after a charge of madness has been answered.

links.why: the identical sentence closing another surah
the same words placed directly after the same charge is dismissed

28.sense: The reminder is for everyone, and it does its work in whoever wants it to. No one is excluded by the previous verse and nobody is carried by this one. The narrowing is done by the person.

notes.t: Yastaqim shares its root with the straight road asked for in Al-Fatiha. The verb is to stand upright and hold that position, so the request is not for a single decision but for a posture that is kept.

Surat al-Muddaththir puts the same two statements in the same order, human willing first and then the divine will that contains it, which suggests the pairing is a settled way of speaking rather than a one-off.

links.why: whoever wills remembers it, and they will not unless Allah wills
the identical pairing closing another surah

29.sense: The last verse takes nothing back from the one before it and puts a frame round it. The wanting in verse twenty eight is real and belongs to the person. The capacity to want anything at all sits inside a will that is not his. The surah ends on the title Al-Fatiha opens with.

notes.t: The two verses are built to be read together and neither survives alone. Verse twenty eight without twenty nine makes a human will that runs on its own supply. Verse twenty nine without twenty eight makes it a fiction. The order is human first, which is where the responsibility is left.
The theologians divided sharply over how the two wills relate, and the schools that formed around the question are still distinguishable. The Qur'an affirms both and does not describe the mechanism.
notes.src: a long-running difference between the theological schools over the relation of the two wills

notes.t: The same sentence, word for word, closes Surat al-Insan, again immediately after a verse granting the choice to whoever wants it.

links.why: the identical closing sentence in the identical position
the surah closes on the name the Book opens with, Lord of the worlds

1.sense: One word, standing as an entire verse. Qar is a knock, a blow that lands with a noise, and the surah names the Hour by the sound it makes on arrival rather than by what it is.

notes.t: The root q-r-a means to strike, and a miqraa is a stick used for beating. The word works on the ear before it works on the mind, which is part of why the surah spends two more verses withholding the explanation.
The Qur'an uses the same name of the disaster that struck Thamud and Ad, so the word already had a history with the audience before it was spent on the Hour.

links.why: Thamud and Ad denied the striking blow, and the word is used of what hit them
the same word used of a calamity that keeps landing on people in this life

2.sense: The name is said and then immediately questioned, as though the word had not managed to carry it. The Qur'an uses this shape when a thing is being introduced that the listener has no experience to attach it to.

notes.t: A question asked about a word the speaker has only just said tells the hearer that his first understanding of it was too small. The device does its work before any content arrives.
Surat al-Haqqa opens with the same three steps in the same order: the name, then what is it, then what will make you know what it is. The pattern is a set form and not an improvisation here.

links.why: the same opening in three steps, on a different name for the same Day
the same withholding question asked about Saqar

3.sense: The question turns and is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ himself. Whatever the audience thinks it has taken in, the man receiving the revelation is told he has been handed the word and not the thing.

notes.t: Wherever the Qur'an says what has made you know, an explanation follows. Where it says what will make you perceive, the matter is left closed, and the Hour's timing is one of the things left there. Here the explanation comes, and it is two similes rather than a definition.
The construction is used more than a dozen times in the Qur'an, and almost always about something on the far side of death, which is the only category where the audience has no evidence of its own.

links.why: the same question asked twice about the Day of Recompense
the same question comes back later in this surah about a different word

4.sense: The answer is a picture, not a definition. Farash are the small insects that pour toward a lamp at night, all of them moving, none of them going anywhere on purpose. Everybody is in motion and nobody is steering.

notes.t: The classical lexicons describe farash as the creatures that throw themselves into a flame. If that association is being used, the simile already contains the ending of the surah in it.
Mabthuth means strewn, sown, spread out by scattering. It is the word for seed thrown by hand, so the crowd has no formation and no leader in it.

A nearby surah gives the same scene with a different insect, people coming out of the graves like locusts spreading, which is a swarm with direction. The two images are not identical and the Qur'an keeps both.

links.why: coming out of the graves like locusts spreading out
hurrying out as though racing toward a marker set up for them

5.sense: Ihn is dyed wool, and manfush is wool pulled apart on the comb until it will lift in a draught. The heaviest fixed things in the landscape end as the lightest thing in a household.

notes.t: Nafsh is a domestic action done by hand, ordinarily by women working wool in the tent. The Qur'an puts a household verb against a cosmic subject, and the mismatch is the point of the line.
The colour in ihn is not decorative. Some exegetes take the dyed wool as carrying the shades of the mountains themselves, which the Qur'an elsewhere describes as streaked white and red and black.
notes.src: the exegetes differ on whether the colour in ihn is intended; compare 35:27

notes.t: Surat al-Maarij gives the same comparison in two words, so it is a fixed image in the Qur'an rather than one built for this surah.

links.why: the sky like molten metal and the mountains like wool, in the same pairing
the same mountains scattered and the ground left flat

6.sense: The sorting is done by weight and not by count. Two people can hand in the same number of deeds and the pans still come to rest in different places, because the question asked of the pile is what it weighs.

notes.t: The Prophet ﷺ said that two words are light on the tongue and heavy on the scale and beloved to the Most Merciful: subhan Allah wa bihamdih, subhan Allah al-azim. The report makes the point about weight against volume as plainly as it can be made.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from Abu Hurayra, at the close of the Book of Tawhid in Bukhari

notes.t: What exactly is weighed was disputed. Reports and arguments were advanced for the deeds themselves, for the pages the deeds are recorded on, and for the person who did them. The scholars did not settle it, and the Qur'an speaks only of the pans.
notes.src: Ibn Hajar collects the three positions and the evidence advanced for each

notes.t: The plural mawazin is used rather than the singular, and the exegetes read it either as many scales or as the many things weighed in one.

links.why: the weighing that Day is the truth, with both outcomes stated
the same two verdicts given in the same order

7.sense: The Arabic says a contented life, putting the contentment in the life rather than in the man living it. English has to say a life he is pleased with, which loses the move the Arabic makes.

notes.t: Radiyah is the active participle, so the life is doing the being-pleased. The grammarians treat this as a transfer of the description from the person to the thing, and it produces a life that is satisfying by its own nature rather than by his adjusting to it.
The identical phrase appears in Surat al-Haqqa, said of the man handed his record in his right hand, which fixes who is meant here without this surah having to say it.

links.why: the same phrase, with the invitation to eat and drink for what you sent ahead
faces at ease that day, pleased with what their striving produced

8.sense: Light, not empty. The pan may be holding something and still fail to move. The verse does not say the man brought nothing. It says what he brought did not weigh, which is the harder sentence of the two.

notes.t: Lightness rather than emptiness is the sharper reading and the one the word supports. A life full of visible activity can arrive at the scale and register almost nothing.
The Qur'an describes people whose effort in this life went to waste while they thought they were doing well, and says that no weight will be set up for them on that Day.

links.why: the greatest losers in works, who believed they were producing something
the light scales explained as the loss of the self

9.sense: His mother is an abyss. The Arabic reaches for the one word that names a place of shelter and safety and puts a bottomless pit in it, and the sentence is only two words long.

notes.t: Most exegetes read umm here as refuge and dwelling, since the Arabs called what a man returns to and rests in his umm. On that reading the shock is deliberate: the word for the safest place a person knows is used for the least safe.
notes.src: at-Tabari records this reading and also the minority one in which umm is the crown of the head, the man falling into the pit headfirst

notes.t: Hawiyah comes from hawa, to fall. The Fire is being named by the falling rather than by the burning, and the burning is held back until the last verse.
The Qur'an gives the Fire a number of names across the surahs, and several of them, like this one, describe an action rather than a substance.

links.why: another surah naming the Fire by what it does, the crusher that reaches the hearts
the one who associates partners pictured as falling out of the sky

10.sense: The withholding question is asked a second time, now about the abyss rather than the striking. The extra letter at the end, the silent ha, is written into the Mushaf and gives the line a stop you can hear.

notes.t: The letter is called ha as-sakt, the ha of pause. It carries no meaning of its own and exists so that the voice has somewhere to land. It is written in only a handful of places in the Qur'an, several of them in Surat al-Haqqa.
The canonical reciters differ over whether the ha is sounded when this verse is joined to the next without stopping. It is sounded when the reciter stops on it.
notes.src: a difference among the canonical reciters over joining and pausing on the ha of pause

links.why: the same silent ha written at the end of several verses in one passage
the first time the question was asked, seven verses earlier

11.sense: Two words and the surah stops. After being asked twice what it is, the answer is the plainest one available: fire, hot. Nothing is elaborated, and the shortness of it is the last thing the listener is left with.

notes.t: Everything before this verse was simile. People were like moths, mountains were like wool. This is not a comparison, and the change of register at the end is doing the work that a longer description would have failed to do.
The same word for the fire is used in Surat al-Ghashiya of what the labouring, weary faces are made to enter.

links.why: the same word for the fire, with what is given to drink and eat there
the fire of Allah, kindled, that mounts up over the hearts

1.sense: The surah opens with a question about an event the city dated its calendar by. Have you not seen is not about eyesight. It is the Arabic for a thing you know as securely as if you had watched it, and the audience did know it.

notes.t: The whole argument is carried by one word, rabbuka. The Makkans did not need to be told what happened to the army. They needed to be told whose act it was, and the verse names Him as the Lord of the man they were arguing with.

The Prophet ﷺ said on the day Makka was taken that Allah had held the elephant back from Makka and given His Messenger and the believers authority over it. The event is treated in the hadith as a known historical fact, not a parable.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from the sermon given on the day Makka was taken

notes.t: The story behind the surah, Abraha and his church in Sanaa and his march north, comes from the sira literature, chiefly Ibn Ishaq. That material is transmitted history rather than hadith, and its details carry the weight that history carries.
notes.src: Ibn Ishaq as transmitted by Ibn Hisham, and the early historians; sira material, not a graded report

links.why: the same opening construction used of Ad, have you not seen how your Lord dealt with them
the surah that follows, which reads as the consequence of this one

2.sense: The plan is not called defeated. It is called lost. Tadlil is the causing of a thing to wander off its road, so the army arrived and the scheme did not arrive at what it was aimed at.

notes.t: Kayd is a plan made quietly and carried out against someone who does not know it is coming. The answer given to it here is not counter-force. The plan is simply sent off course, which is a cheaper defeat and a more humiliating one.
The Qur'an uses the same framing elsewhere: they plan and Allah plans, and He is the best of planners, and the scheme of those who reject is nothing but astray.

links.why: they plan and Allah plans, and He is the best of those who plan
a plan big enough to move mountains, and where it ended up

3.sense: The army had an elephant, which was the largest instrument of war anyone in that part of the world had seen. What came against it was birds. The mismatch is not an ornament of the story, it is the argument the surah is making.

notes.t: Ababil has no agreed singular, and the philologists differ over whether it is a plural without one. What they agree on is the sense: successive groups, flock behind flock, arriving in waves rather than all at once.
notes.src: the philologists differ over the word's form; at-Tabari records several accounts of its derivation

notes.t: The Qur'an does not say what the birds looked like, how big they were or what species they belonged to. Later storytellers supplied all of that. The verse supplies none of it.
Small creatures used as an army is a pattern in the Qur'an rather than a one-off. Pharaoh's people were sent the flood, the locusts, the lice and the frogs, each named as a distinct sign.

links.why: locusts, lice and frogs sent as detailed signs against a stronger power
the flimsiest of houses set against the strongest of confidences

4.sense: The birds carry stones and throw them. The word for the stones is the one the Qur'an uses for what was rained on the people of Lut, which files this event in the same drawer as that one without saying so.

notes.t: Sijjil is generally explained as hardened or baked clay. Some early philologists derived the word from a Persian compound meaning stone and clay, and the lexicons preserve the discussion without closing it.
notes.src: the lexicographers and early philologists differ over the derivation; at-Tabari reports the accounts

notes.t: The verb tarmi is singular and continuous, describing the throwing as it happens rather than reporting it as finished. The Arabic keeps the reader inside the event for one line.

links.why: stones of sijjil rained in layers on the people of Lut
the same word for the same rain, in another telling

5.sense: Asf is the husk and leaf left on a grain stalk after the grain has gone, and makul says it has been eaten. The army ends as what is left on a stable floor once the animals have finished, which is not a body and not a ruin but a residue.

notes.t: The last word of the surah is the least dignified one available. Nothing in the line grants the army the standing of a defeated enemy, and that refusal is the closing move.

Asf appears elsewhere in the Qur'an in an entirely ordinary sense, among the things the earth produces, grain with its husk and fragrant plants. The word carries no menace of its own; the context supplies all of it.

Whether this surah and Surat Quraysh are one surah or two was discussed by the early scholars, and the mushaf of Ubayy ibn Kab is reported to have joined them without a separating line. The reading in general use keeps them apart.
notes.src: reports about the mushaf of Ubayy ibn Kab and the positions of the early scholars; the received arrangement separates them

links.why: another people left like the dry sticks of a stockman's pen
what the Quraysh were left holding once the army was gone
